status: DRAFT - for content validation by >= 3 practising midwifery/obstetric experts (Section 3.5)
notes: Thresholds (N, s, cm, progress-rate) are initial estimates to be calibrated against the expert-annotated reference recordings (Section 3.2). Edit freely; place an edited copy in persistentDataPath/NeonatalDelivery/ to override without rebuilding.

rules.name: Unsupported cranium
rules.complication: Rapid, uncontrolled birth of the head: 2nd-3rd degree perineal tear (obstetric anal sphincter injury) and risk of neonatal intracranial haemorrhage from sudden decompression.
rules.explanation: Without a hand on the occiput the head extends early and is expelled quickly, so a larger diameter distends the perineum abruptly instead of gradually.
rules.remediation: Rest the flat fingers of your dominant hand on the occiput and apply gentle pressure to keep the head flexed; ask the mother to pant and let the head be born slowly between contractions.
rules.source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2nd ed., 2017) - normal vaginal delivery; WHO/HEAT labour & delivery care module; RCOG Green-top Guideline No.29 (3rd/4th degree perineal tears); RCOG/RCM OASI Care Bundle - manual perineal protection

rules.name: Excessive pressure on the fetal head
rules.complication: Prolonged compression of the fetal skull: fetal heart rate decelerations and a delayed, obstructed birth of the head.
rules.explanation: Controlling the speed of delivery needs only light pressure; pushing the head back works against the contraction and compresses the skull.
rules.remediation: Use gentle, flat-finger pressure - enough to slow the head, never to hold it back.
rules.source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2nd ed., 2017) - normal vaginal delivery; WHO/HEAT labour & delivery care module

rules.name: Perineum not supported
rules.complication: Unsupported perineum during crowning: increased risk of perineal tear.
rules.explanation: Manual perineal protection with the other hand (thumb and index on either side of the perineum) reduces the stretch on the posterior fourchette as the head extends.
rules.remediation: With your non-dominant hand hold a pad on the perineum below the introitus while the head is born.
rules.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No.29 (3rd/4th degree perineal tears); RCOG/RCM OASI Care Bundle - manual perineal protection

rules.name: Pressure on the face / eyes
rules.complication: Facial bruising and risk of ocular injury.
rules.explanation: The face is born last by extension; pressure should be applied only to the bony occiput and parietal bones.
rules.remediation: Keep your fingers on the occiput / parietal bones, away from the eyes and face.
rules.source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2nd ed., 2017) - normal vaginal delivery; WHO/HEAT labour & delivery care module

rules.name: Neck not checked for a nuchal cord
rules.complication: An undetected tight nuchal cord can tighten as the body is born: cord compression, hypoxia and a floppy, cyanosed newborn.
rules.explanation: After the head is born you must feel around the neck; a loose loop is slipped over the head, a tight one is managed before delivery continues.
rules.remediation: Slide two fingers along the baby's neck to feel for a loop of cord before the next contraction.
rules.source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2nd ed., 2017) - normal vaginal delivery; WHO/HEAT labour & delivery care module

rules.name: Traction before external rotation
rules.complication: Pulling before the shoulders have rotated into the antero-posterior diameter: anterior shoulder impaction (shoulder dystocia).
rules.explanation: Restitution and external rotation are spontaneous; traction before they complete drags the bisacromial diameter against the pubic arch.
rules.remediation: Keep your hands still and only support the head until it has rotated to face the mother's thigh.
rules.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No.42 (shoulder dystocia); NHS Scotland shoulder dystocia guideline (2026): routine AXIAL traction only; downward/excessive traction inappropriate

rules.name: Wrong axis of traction
rules.complication: Brachial plexus stretch injury (Erb's palsy, C5-C6): arm held in the 'waiter's tip' position.
rules.explanation: Traction that is not in line with the fetal spine laterally flexes the neck and stretches the upper roots of the brachial plexus.
rules.remediation: Hold the head on both parietal bones and apply gentle AXIAL traction in line with the fetal spine (no downward or sideways pull).
rules.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No.42 (shoulder dystocia); NHS Scotland shoulder dystocia guideline (2026): routine AXIAL traction only; downward/excessive traction inappropriate

rules.name: Excessive traction force
rules.complication: Excessive traction: brachial plexus injury and clavicle fracture risk.
rules.explanation: The shoulders are delivered by the contraction and maternal effort; traction should be gentle and only guide the direction.
rules.remediation: Reduce your pull to gentle guidance and wait for the next contraction.
rules.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No.42 (shoulder dystocia); NHS Scotland shoulder dystocia guideline (2026): routine AXIAL traction only; downward/excessive traction inappropriate

rules.name: Pulling on the neck
rules.complication: Traction transmitted through the neck: cervical spine and carotid compression injury.
rules.explanation: The neck must never be gripped; the head is held over the parietal bones (biparietal hold).
rules.remediation: Move your hands up onto the parietal bones on either side of the head.
rules.source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2nd ed., 2017) - normal vaginal delivery; WHO/HEAT labour & delivery care module

rules.name: Excessive lateral flexion of the neck
rules.complication: Lateral flexion of the neck stretches the brachial plexus on the opposite side (Erb's palsy).
rules.explanation: Sideways force bends the cervical spine away from the shoulder and over-stretches C5-C6.
rules.remediation: Keep the head in line with the spine - pull along the axis, never sideways.
rules.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No.42 (shoulder dystocia); NHS Scotland shoulder dystocia guideline (2026): routine AXIAL traction only; downward/excessive traction inappropriate

rules.name: Finger hooked in the axilla
rules.complication: Axillary traction: brachial plexus and humerus injury.
rules.explanation: Pulling on the arm pit concentrates force on the plexus and humerus.
rules.remediation: Support the body along the back and buttocks instead of pulling under the arm.
rules.source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No.42 (shoulder dystocia); NHS Scotland shoulder dystocia guideline (2026): routine AXIAL traction only; downward/excessive traction inappropriate

rules.name: Posterior shoulder delivered in the wrong direction
rules.complication: Uncontrolled posterior shoulder: perineal tear extension.
rules.explanation: Once the anterior shoulder is free the posterior shoulder follows the curve of the birth canal upward; pulling downward drags it across the perineum.
rules.remediation: Guide the head gently upward (anteriorly), following the curve, while watching the perineum.
rules.source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2nd ed., 2017) - normal vaginal delivery; WHO/HEAT labour & delivery care module; RCOG Green-top Guideline No.29 (3rd/4th degree perineal tears); RCOG/RCM OASI Care Bundle - manual perineal protection

rules.name: Premature release during birth of the body
rules.complication: The slippery newborn is unsupported as the body is born and can slip or fall.
rules.explanation: The body delivers quickly by lateral flexion; one hand must support the head/neck and the other slide along the back to the buttocks.
rules.remediation: Keep one hand under the head and neck and slide the other along the back to grasp the buttocks/legs as the body is born.
rules.source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2nd ed., 2017) - normal vaginal delivery; WHO/HEAT labour & delivery care module

rules.name: Newborn held with one hand
rules.complication: Unsupported head and neck: risk of a fall and of neck hyperextension.
rules.explanation: A newborn has no head control; always use two hands until it is on the mother's chest.
rules.remediation: Hold the baby with both hands - one under the head/neck, one under the buttocks.
rules.source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2nd ed., 2017) - normal vaginal delivery; WHO/HEAT labour & delivery care module

rules.name: Newborn released away from the mother
rules.complication: Newborn fall: head injury, fractures.
rules.explanation: Release the baby only once it is resting securely on the mother's chest.
rules.remediation: Carry the baby with both hands and place it prone on the mother's chest before letting go.
rules.source: WHO Managing Complications in Pregnancy and Childbirth (2nd ed., 2017) - normal vaginal delivery; WHO/HEAT labour & delivery care module

rules.name: Early cord clamping
rules.complication: Placental transfusion lost: lower blood volume and iron stores in infancy.
rules.explanation: WHO recommends clamping no earlier than 1 minute after birth (unless resuscitation is needed); the cord transfuses blood while it pulsates.
rules.remediation: Wait at least one minute (until the cord stops pulsating) before applying the clamps.
rules.source: WHO guideline: delayed umbilical cord clamping (2014) - not earlier than 1 min; WHO/HEAT: first tie/clamp ~2 finger-widths (~3 cm), second ~5 cm, cut between

rules.name: First clamp misplaced
rules.complication: Clamp too close to the skin risks catching the umbilical skin or a small umbilical hernia; too far leaves a long stump that bleeds and becomes infected.
rules.explanation: The first clamp goes about two finger-widths (~3 cm) from the abdomen.
rules.remediation: Place the first clamp about 3 cm from the umbilicus.
rules.source: WHO guideline: delayed umbilical cord clamping (2014) - not earlier than 1 min; WHO/HEAT: first tie/clamp ~2 finger-widths (~3 cm), second ~5 cm, cut between

rules.name: Second clamp misplaced
rules.complication: Second clamp misplaced: uncontrolled bleeding from the cut placental end.
rules.explanation: The second clamp sits ~5 cm from the abdomen so the cord can be cut safely between the clamps.
rules.remediation: Place the second clamp about 2 cm beyond the first (~5 cm from the abdomen).
rules.source: WHO guideline: delayed umbilical cord clamping (2014) - not earlier than 1 min; WHO/HEAT: first tie/clamp ~2 finger-widths (~3 cm), second ~5 cm, cut between

rules.name: Clamps too close / too far apart
rules.complication: Insufficient space to cut between the clamps safely.
rules.explanation: Leave about 2 cm between the clamps.
rules.remediation: Re-site the clamps about 2 cm apart.
rules.source: WHO guideline: delayed umbilical cord clamping (2014) - not earlier than 1 min; WHO/HEAT: first tie/clamp ~2 finger-widths (~3 cm), second ~5 cm, cut between

rules.name: Cord cut without two clamps
rules.complication: Neonatal haemorrhage from the unclamped umbilical vessels.
rules.explanation: Both sides of the cut must be clamped before cutting.
rules.remediation: Apply two clamps first, then cut between them.
rules.source: WHO guideline: delayed umbilical cord clamping (2014) - not earlier than 1 min; WHO/HEAT: first tie/clamp ~2 finger-widths (~3 cm), second ~5 cm, cut between

rules.name: Cut outside the clamps
rules.complication: Cutting on the baby's side of the first clamp causes neonatal bleeding; beyond the second clamp, bleeding from the placental end.
rules.explanation: The only safe place to cut is between the two clamps.
rules.remediation: Position the scissor blades between the clamps, shield with your other hand, then cut.
rules.source: WHO guideline: delayed umbilical cord clamping (2014) - not earlier than 1 min; WHO/HEAT: first tie/clamp ~2 finger-widths (~3 cm), second ~5 cm, cut between
